newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela's diplomatic roller-coaster hits Mideast.
newsitem.headline: Mandela's diplomatic roller-coaster hits Mideast.

text.p: Careening unpredictably around the globe, South African foreign policy collided with the Middle East this week and pitched straight into a diplomatic mess over plans to help Syria modernise its battle tanks.
Opposition parties and commentators, blanching at Pretoria's latest faux-pas in international affairs, called it a gauche, puerile and flaky performance -- as well as a bad idea.
Some analysts said the embarrassment may have been a U.S. move to sabotage the South African arms industry.

And less than 24 hours after his government appeared to row back on the controversial arms tender, a defiant President Nelson Mandela said South Africa would sell arms to whomever it chose, whether or not they were approved by the West.

It was a weekend leak of secret South African cabinet documents, possibly by the U.S. spy agency CIA according to one daily paper, which blew the whistle on the plan to export advanced weaponry to Syria for $641 million.
The United States, admitting it was already aware of the proposal and had tried to talk South Africa out of it, threatened to withdraw financial aid if the deal went ahead.
The United States accuses Syria of sponsoring terrorism, something Damascus denies.
South Africa has enjoyed something of a pet-pupil relationship with the United States since the "miracle transition" to majority rule and the election of Mandela.

Vice-president Al Gore, who co-chairs a U.S.-S.A. Binational Commission, is due to visit South Africa next month. But this outburst of mutual suspicion and public recrimination could now throw that gesture, if not the commission, into doubt.
The row could also add to pressure for a shakeup at the foreign ministry, with persistent speculation centering on a reshuffle that would retire Foreign Minister Alfred Nzo.

Analysts say that the ineffectual Nzo leaves foreign policy in the hands of Mandela and his deputy Thabo Mbeki, a dangerously ad hoc system that has led to a roller-coaster of seemingly off-the-cuff decisions.

On Tuesday, a Mandela spokesman complained about public American bullying but the incipient row appeared to be defused later the same day when the Foreign Ministry sniffily denied that it had authorized any arms "contract" per se.
A spokesman also pointed out, hair-splittingly, that only a bid to sell Syria non-lethal "software" was approved.
Everywhere but in the government, it seems, the bid to provide accuracy-enhancing gear for Syrian tanks set off alarms, and Mandela's government was hammered by Wednesday's press.

The government's handling of the proposed deal, and of its unplanned revelation, was fatuous, undiplomatic and petulant, said Johannesburg's daily The Citizen. It was also ill-considered, embarrassing and perverse, in the words of Business Day.

Six weeks ago, foreign policy analysts were appalled at Mandela's abrupt switch of diplomatic allegiance from Taiwan to Beijing, which smashed much diplomatic china and reversed his own pledge never to abandon plucky Taipei.
"As a foreign policy shock this (Syria plan) goes way beyond the inconsistent approach to the two Chinas," said Business Day.

"Given the not unexpected hard line emanating from the U.S. and the initial, ill-considered 'Yankee go home' reaction...it is difficult to see how government can creep away from the mess without losing face," the paper judged.

Analysts were divided over whether the government is bent on helping South Africa's weapons-makers earn export dollars, or sending out an ideological statement to underscore support for the Arab cause, or a combination of both.
But Mandela's blast on Wednesday added two more explosive ingredients to the puzzling policy mix -- injured pride and old loyalties.

"We will never allow any support or assistance from any country, no matter how powerful it is, to dictate our foreign policy, nor allow any country to violate our sovereignty amd undermine our national pride," the president said.
In a sobering reminder to Western allies that he counts Libya, Cuba, Iran and Iraq among his friends, the 78-year-old leader said: "the enemies of...the West are not our enemies".

Advocates of "realpolitik" may have to revise hopes that South Africa can quickly be weaned away from loyalty to countries that supported the black liberation struggle against apartheid, whether or not they are seen as pariahs elsewhere.

"A little country with huge problems...should mind its own business," said columnist Simon Barber, in a blistering attack on the foreign policy "piety" of Mandela's ruling African National Congress (ANC).

"Piss off the richest, most powerful nation on earth, and not only do you become suspect to its own capitalists but the cost of your money becomes dearer as the superpower's friends and clients begin to see you as flaky," Barber warned, as the bond market quailed under the impact of the dispute.
